Each capsule contains lactose anhydrous and sulfur dioxide.

formulations.label: Powder for oral suspension
formulations.note: Contains sucrose (3.9 g per 5 mL), glucose and a trace of benzyl alcohol.

src.q: containing the equivalent of 200 mg azithromycin base, on reconstitution with water
Each 5 ml (200 mg) of reconstituted powder for oral suspension contains 3.9 g sucrose, 28.0 mg glucose and 0.35 μg of benzyl alcohol.

items.t: Adults and adolescents (12 to 17 years) weighing at least 45 kg: acute streptococcal tonsillitis/pharyngitis, acute bacterial sinusitis, acute bacterial otitis media, community-acquired pneumonia, acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections, urethritis/cervicitis due to Chlamydia trachomatis, and (with another antibacterial, e.g. ceftriaxone) due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Adults only: acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis.
items.tag: Capsules (and suspension if unable to swallow)

src.q: Adults (18 years of age and above) and adolescents (12 - 17 years of age) weighing at least 45 kg - Acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis - Acute bacterial sinusitis - Acute bacterial otitis media - Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)
Acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI) - Urethritis and cervicitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis
Adults (18 years of age and above) only - Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis (AECB)

items.t: Children from 6 months weighing under 45 kg: acute bacterial sinusitis, acute bacterial otitis media, community-acquired pneumonia, acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections. From 2 years: acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis.

src.q: Paediatric patients aged 6 months and older and weighing less than 45 kg - Acute bacterial sinusitis - Acute bacterial otitis media - Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) - Acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI)
Paediatric patients aged 2 years and older and weighing less than 45 kg - Acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis

items.t: Start only after careful benefit/risk assessment considering local resistance, and when preferred regimens are not indicated (risk of resistance).

src.q: Treatment with azithromycin should only be initiated after a careful assessment of the benefit and the risks, considering the local prevalence of resistance, and when preferred treatment regimens are not indicated.

items.t: Not recommended for uncomplicated gonorrhoea or pelvic inflammatory disease unless lab results confirm susceptibility.

src.q: azithromycin is not recommended for the treatment of uncomplicated gonorrhoea and pelvic inflammatory disease unless laboratory results have confirmed susceptibility of the organism to azithromycin

items.t: Tonsillitis/pharyngitis, sinusitis, otitis media, AECB (adults only), community-acquired pneumonia, skin and skin structure infections: 500 mg/day for 3 days, or 500 mg on day 1 then 250 mg/day on days 2 to 5. Single daily dose.

src.q: 500 mg/day for 3 days or 500 mg on day 1, followed by 250 mg/day on days 2-5
Azithromycin should be administered as a single daily dose.

items.t: Urethritis/cervicitis due to Chlamydia trachomatis: 1000 mg as a single dose.

src.q: Urethritis and cervicitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis 1000 mg as a single dose

items.t: Urethritis/cervicitis due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae (with another antibacterial, e.g. ceftriaxone): 1000 mg, or 2000 mg in adults only, as a single dose.

src.q: 1000 mg or 2000 mg* as a single dose * for treatment of adults only

items.t: Missed dose: if 12 hours or less late, take it as soon as possible; if more than 12 hours, wait for the next scheduled dose.

src.q: If 12 hours or less have passed since the missed dose, the patient should be advised to take it as soon as possible
If more than 12 hours have passed since the time the dose is usually taken, the patient should be advised to wait until the next scheduled dose.

items.t: Elderly: no dose adjustment, but particular caution because of arrhythmia and torsades de pointes risk.

src.q: Since the elderly are more likely to experience proarrhythmic conditions, particular caution is recommended due to the risk of developing cardiac arrhythmia and torsades de pointes

items.t: Children 6 months and older under 45 kg, sinusitis, community-acquired pneumonia, skin and skin structure infections: 10 mg/kg/day for 3 days, or 10 mg/kg on day 1 then 5 mg/kg/day on days 2 to 5. Single daily dose.

src.q: Acute bacterial sinusitis Community-acquired pneumonia Acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections 10 mg/kg/day for 3 days or 10 mg/kg on day 1, followed by 5 mg/kg/day on days 2-5

items.t: Acute otitis media: single dose of 30 mg/kg (maximum total 1500 mg), or 10 mg/kg/day for 3 days, or 10 mg/kg on day 1 then 5 mg/kg/day on days 2 to 5.

src.q: Acute bacterial otitis media single dose of 30 mg/kg or 10 mg/kg/day for 3 days or 10 mg/kg on day 1, followed by 5 mg/kg/day on days 2-5
with exception of the 1-day treatment course (single dose) for acute bacterial otitis media for which the maximum total dose of 1500 mg should not be exceeded

items.t: Acute streptococcal tonsillitis/pharyngitis (2 years and older): 20 mg/kg/day for 3 days or 12 mg/kg/day for 5 days.

src.q: Acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis* 20 mg/kg/day for 3 days or 12 mg/kg/day for 5 days

items.t: Daily dose must not exceed the adult 500 mg/day (except the single-dose otitis media course). Maximum total dose for any course under 45 kg is 1500 mg, except the 5-day tonsillitis/pharyngitis regimen.

src.q: The azithromycin daily dose should not exceed the adult daily dose of 500 mg
The maximum recommended total dose for any treatment for paediatric patients weighing less than 45 kg is 1500 mg, except for the 5-day regimen for acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis.

items.t: Safety and efficacy not established under 6 months. Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis reported after use in the first 42 days of life.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of azithromycin have not been established in children under 6 months of age for any of the indications listed in section 4.1.
Cases of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis have been reported following the administration of azithromycin for the first 42 days after birth.

items.t: Capsules: for adults and adolescents weighing at least 45 kg; other forms are more suitable for children under 45 kg or those unable to swallow capsules.

src.q: Other pharmaceutical forms are available that may be more appropriate to treat patients unable to swallow capsules as well as paediatric patients weighing less than 45 kg.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to azithromycin, erythromycin, any macrolide or ketolide antibiotic, or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, erythromycin, any macrolide or ketolide antibiotic, or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes: use with caution in ongoing proarrhythmic conditions (especially women and the elderly), e.g. congenital or documented QT prolongation, other QT-prolonging medicines, electrolyte disturbance (especially hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia), clinically relevant bradycardia, arrhythmia or severe cardiac insufficiency.

src.q: azithromycin should be used with caution in patients with ongoing proarrhythmic conditions (especially women and elderly patients) such as patients: With congenital or documented QT prolongation
With electrolyte disturbance, particularly in case of hypokalaemia and hypomagnesemia With clinically relevant bradycardia, cardiac arrhythmia or severe cardiac insufficiency

items.t: SPS (macrolides): no ECG needed when used alone without risk factors. Do not prescribe with a history of QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmia or significant electrolyte disturbance. Monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during treatment if there are non-modifiable risk factors.

src.q: Macrolides Management No ECG monitoring is required when used alone and in the absence of risk factors. Do not prescribe in people with a history of QT interval prolongation, ventricular arrhythmia, or significant electrolyte disturbance.
Monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during treatment in people with non-modifiable patient and medicine risk factors.

items.t: Hepatotoxicity (fulminant hepatitis, hepatic failure, some fatal): caution in significant hepatic disease. Stop and check liver function if signs of liver dysfunction develop.

src.q: the use of azithromycin should be undertaken with caution in patients with significant hepatic disease
Patients should be advised to stop azithromycin administration and to contact their physician if signs and symptoms of liver dysfunction

items.t: Severe hypersensitivity and SCARs (SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP): advise patients and monitor closely; stop if an allergic reaction occurs. Symptoms may recur after symptomatic treatment stops.

src.q: If an allergic reaction occurs, azithromycin should be discontinued, and appropriate therapy should be instituted.
Physicians should be aware that reappearance of the allergic symptoms may occur when symptomatic therapy is discontinued.

items.t: Myasthenia gravis: exacerbations and new myasthenic syndrome reported.

src.q: Exacerbations of the symptoms of myasthenia gravis and new onset of myasthenia syndrome have been reported in patients receiving azithromycin therapy

items.t: C. difficile diarrhoea / pseudomembranous colitis: consider stopping; do not give medicines that inhibit peristalsis.

src.q: Medicinal products that inhibit peristalsis should not be given.

items.t: Sexually transmitted infections: exclude Mycoplasma genitalium co-infection before single-dose treatment, and exclude syphilis.

src.q: concomitant urogenital infection by Mycoplasma genitalium should be excluded due to the high risk of emergence of resistance in this organism
a concomitant infection caused by Treponema pallidum should be excluded

items.t: Ergot derivatives: should not be co-administered (theoretical ergotism).

src.q: azithromycin and ergot derivatives should not be co-administrated

items.t: Capsules contain lactose (patients with hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take them) and sulfur dioxide (may rarely cause severe hypersensitivity and bronchospasm).

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
Zithromax capsules contains sulfur dioxide which may rarely cause severe hypersensitivity reactions and bronchospasm.

items.t: Suspension contains sucrose and glucose: patients with hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicinal product.

items.t: QT-prolonging medicines (e.g. class IA/III antiarrhythmics, pimozide, citalopram, fluoroquinolones such as moxifloxacin and levofloxacin, chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine): use with caution.

src.q: Azithromycin should be used with caution in patients receiving medicinal products known to prolong the QT interval
fluoroquinolones (e.g. moxifloxacin and levofloxacin), cisapride, chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine

items.t: Hydroxychloroquine: MHRA says co-administration with azithromycin in rheumatoid arthritis was linked to more cardiovascular events and cardiovascular deaths; carefully weigh benefits and risks before prescribing.

src.q: Carefully consider the benefits and risks before prescribing systemic azithromycin or other systemic macrolide antibiotics (erythromycin or clarithromycin) to patients being treated with hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine.

items.t: Statins (e.g. atorvastatin): rhabdomyolysis reported after marketing; exercise caution. SPS: statins can be continued with azithromycin; counsel patients to report unexpected side effects.

src.q: Caution should be exercised since post-marketing cases of rhabdomyolysis in patients receiving azithromycin concomitantly with statins have been reported.
Azithromycin can be given concomitantly with statins. However, counsel patients to report any unexpected side effects.

items.t: Warfarin and other coumarins: potentiated anticoagulation reported; consider more frequent prothrombin time monitoring during and after treatment.

src.q: post-marketing reports of potentiated anticoagulation of coumarin-type oral anticoagulants upon co-administration with azithromycin
A higher frequency of prothrombin time monitoring should be considered during and after treatment with azithromycin.

items.t: No clinically relevant change in studies with antacids (aluminium/magnesium hydroxide), carbamazepine, cetirizine, fluconazole, sildenafil or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.

src.q: No clinically relevant change in the exposure of azithromycin or the co-administered medicinal products was observed in clinical studies evaluating potential drug-drug interactions of azithromycin with oral antacids (aluminium hydroxide/magnesium hydroxide), carbamazepine, cetirizine
fluconazole, methylprednisolone, midazolam, rifabutin, sildenafil, theophylline, triazolam, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and zidovudine

items.t: P-gp substrates with a narrow therapeutic index (e.g. digoxin, colchicine, dabigatran, ciclosporin): monitor and adjust as needed during and after treatment.

src.q: For narrow therapeutic index drugs, caution and clinical and/or therapeutic drug monitoring and dose adjustment as appropriate are advised.

items.t: GFR ≥ 10 ml/min: no dose adjustment. GFR < 10 ml/min: use with caution.

src.q: No dose adjustment is necessary in patients with GFR ≥ 10 ml/min. In patients with GFR < 10 ml/min azithromycin should be administered with caution

items.t: Mild or moderate (Child-Pugh A or B): no dose adjustment. Severe (Child-Pugh C): no data; use with caution. Caution in significant hepatic disease.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required in patients with mild (Child-Pugh Class A) or moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class B)
No data is available in patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class C). Therefore, azithromycin should be administered with caution in these patients

items.t: SmPC: observational data (over 7000 exposed pregnancies) mostly show no increased risk of major malformations; miscarriage evidence inconclusive. Use only if clinically needed.

src.q: Most of these studies do not suggest an increased risk of adverse foetal effects such as major congenital malformations or cardiovascular malformations.
Azithromycin should only be used during pregnancy if clinically needed.

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; available information does not show harm.

src.q: Azithromycin can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
The available information does not show that use of azithromycin in pregnancy will harm your baby.

items.t: SmPC: excreted in milk to a substantial extent; diarrhoea, fungal infection and hypersensitivity possible in the infant. Decide whether to stop breastfeeding or stop/avoid azithromycin.

src.q: Azithromycin is excreted in human milk to substantial extent.
A decision must be made whether to discontinue breast-feeding or to discontinue/abstain from azithromycin therapy

items.t: SPS: use with caution; can be used during breastfeeding with precautionary infant monitoring (GI upset, oral thrush, rash, irritability, sleep disturbance, poor feeding).

src.q: Use with caution All formulations of azithromycin, including intravenous therapy can be used during breastfeeding, with precautionary infant monitoring.
monitor for gastro-intestinal disturbances such as diarrhoea and vomiting, oral candida infection, rashes, irritability, sleep disturbances, and loss of appetite

items.t: Reduced pregnancy rates in rat fertility studies; relevance to humans unknown.

src.q: In fertility studies conducted in rat, reduced pregnancy rates were noted following administration of azithromycin. The relevance of this finding to humans is unknown.

items.t: Most commonly reported: diarrhoea, headache, vomiting, abdominal pain, nausea and abnormal laboratory values.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse reactions during treatment include diarrhoea, headache, vomiting, abdominal pain, nausea and abnormal laboratory test values.

items.t: Anaphylaxis, torsades de pointes and arrhythmia (including ventricular tachycardia), pseudomembranous colitis, hepatic failure.

src.q: Other important adverse reactions include anaphylactic reactions, torsades de pointes , arrhythmia including ventricular tachycardia, pseudomembranous colitis and hepatic failure

items.t: SCARs (SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP): stop if an allergic reaction occurs.

src.q: If an allergic reaction occurs, azithromycin should be discontinued, and appropriate therapy should be instituted.

items.t: Liver dysfunction (jaundice, dark urine, bleeding tendency, encephalopathy): stop and check liver function immediately.

src.q: In such cases liver function tests/investigations should be performed immediately.

items.t: Infants: projectile vomiting or irritability with feeding (possible pyloric stenosis) after use in the first 42 days: contact a doctor.

src.q: Parents and caregivers should be asked to contact their doctor if projectile vomiting or irritability with feeding occurs.

items.t: SPS: check ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during treatment when non-modifiable risk factors are present; not needed when used alone without risk factors.

items.t: On warfarin: consider more frequent prothrombin time monitoring during and after treatment. Monitor closely for skin reactions.

src.q: A higher frequency of prothrombin time monitoring should be considered during and after treatment with azithromycin.
At the time of prescription, patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms and monitored closely for skin reactions.

items.t: Stop if an allergic reaction or signs of liver dysfunction occur.

src.q: Patients should be advised to stop azithromycin administration and to contact their physician if signs and symptoms of liver dysfunction

items.t: Capsules: swallow whole, once daily, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal.

src.q: Capsules should be swallowed whole, as a single daily dose, either at least one hour before or two hours after a meal.

items.t: Suspension: once daily with or without a meal (taking just before a meal may improve GI tolerability). Shake before each dose. Use within 5 days of reconstitution.

src.q: Powder for oral suspension should be taken as a single daily dose with or without a meal. Administration immediately before a meal may enhance the gastrointestinal tolerability.
Once reconstituted with water, Zithromax suspension has a shelf-life of 5 days.

items.t: Stop and seek advice for signs of liver problems (yellow skin/eyes, dark urine, bleeding) or allergic/skin reactions.

src.q: Dizziness, drowsiness and convulsions have been reported in some patients taking azithromycin and some patients experienced visual and/or auditory impairment.

items.t: Report diarrhoea during or after the course.

src.q: CDAD and pseudomembranous colitis must be considered in patients who present with diarrhoea during or subsequent to the administration of azithromycin.
